q: Which of these names is a correct IUPAC name?
h: Draw each one. Check for a longer chain hiding in a branch, then check numbering and alphabetical order.
w: 2,3-Dimethylpentane uses the longest chain (five carbons), the lowest locants ({2,3} beats {3,4}) and a single kind of prefix. Each of the others breaks a rule.
x: An ethyl on C2 extends the chain: the compound is 3-methylpentane.
Prefixes must be alphabetical: 3-ethyl-4-methylhexane.
A methyl on C1 lengthens the chain: the compound is 2-methylbutane.

q: To which functional groups do the carbons labeled a and b belong?
h: Look at what each carbonyl carbon is bonded to besides its C=O oxygen.
w: Carbon a is a C=O carbon single-bonded to a ring oxygen that also carries carbon: that is an ester, and because it is part of a ring it is called a lactone. Carbon b is a C=O carbon bonded to two carbons: a ketone.
x: Carbon a is bonded to an O–C oxygen, which makes it an ester, not a ketone; and b carries no H, so it is not an aldehyde.
A carboxylic acid needs an O–H on the carbonyl carbon. Here the oxygen carries a ring carbon instead, which is an ester.
Carbon a has a C=O, so it is part of an ester, not a plain ether; carbon b is bonded to two carbons, so it is a ketone.

q: Epinephrine (adrenaline) is shown. Which choice correctly describes its functional groups?
c: a secondary amine, a secondary alcohol, and two phenol OH groups
a primary amine, a primary alcohol, and two phenol OH groups
a secondary amine, a tertiary alcohol, and two phenol OH groups
an amide, a secondary alcohol, and two phenol OH groups
h: Classify an alcohol by how many carbons are on the C–OH carbon; classify an amine by how many carbons are on N.
w: The nitrogen carries a CH3 and a CH2 (two carbons) and an H: a secondary amine. The side-chain OH carbon is bonded to two carbons (the ring carbon and the CH2), so it is a secondary alcohol. The two OH groups bonded directly to the benzene ring are phenols.
x: The N has two carbon groups (secondary), and the C–OH carbon has two carbon neighbors (secondary).
The C–OH carbon still has one H and two carbon neighbors, which makes it secondary, not tertiary.
There is no carbonyl group, so there is no amide. The nitrogen is an amine.

q:
Morphine is shown. Which statements about its functional groups are correct?
I. It contains a phenol and a secondary alcohol.
II. It contains a tertiary amine.
III. It contains an ester.
h: Find each oxygen and decide what it is bonded to. Then count the carbons on nitrogen.
w: Morphine has three oxygens. One OH is on the benzene ring (phenol). One OH is on a ring CH carbon bonded to two other carbons (secondary alcohol, also allylic). The third O bridges an aromatic carbon and an sp3 carbon with no C=O anywhere, so it is a cyclic ether, not an ester. The N carries three carbons (CH3 and two ring carbons): a tertiary amine. So I and II are true and III is false: I and II only.
x: Statement II is also true: the nitrogen is bonded to three carbons, which makes it a tertiary amine.
Statement III is false: the ring oxygen is an ether. An ester needs a C=O carbon bonded to the O, and morphine has no C=O.
Statement III is false: morphine has no carbonyl group, so it cannot contain an ester.

q: How many degrees of unsaturation does nicotine (shown, C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>14</sub>N<sub>2</sub>) have?
h: Count rings and π bonds, or use the formula: each N adds one to the allowed H count.
w: From the structure: two rings (2) + three π bonds in the pyridine ring (3) = 5. From the formula: (2·10 + 2 + 2 − 14)/2 = 10/2 = 5.
x: This counts the three pyridine π bonds but only one of the two rings. Both rings count.
Three is the π-bond count alone; the two rings each add one more.
This adds an extra unit, as if the formula had two fewer H. Check with (2C + 2 + N − H)/2.

q: A hydrocarbon C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>10</sub> takes up 2 equivalents of H<sub>2</sub> over Pt to give C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>14</sub>. How many rings does it contain?
h: Find the total degrees of unsaturation, then subtract the π bonds that hydrogenation removed.
w: C7H10 has DBE = (14 + 2 − 10)/2 = 3. Hydrogenation over Pt saturates C=C and C≡C bonds but does not open ordinary rings. Two equivalents of H2 account for 2 π bonds, and the product C7H14 still has DBE 1, so the compound has 1 ring.
x: With no rings, C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>10</sub> would add three H<sub>2</sub> to reach C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub>. Only two were taken up.
Two rings would leave only one π bond, so only one H<sub>2</sub> would add.
Three rings would leave no π bonds, so no H<sub>2</sub> would add.

q: Which structure is (E)-4-methylpent-2-en-1-ol?
h: Build the five-carbon chain from the OH carbon (C1), put the C=C between C2 and C3 and the methyl on C4, then check the chain continues trans across the C=C.
w: C1 bears the OH, the double bond is C2=C3 and C4 carries a methyl, so C4 is a CH(CH3)2 unit. On C2 the higher group is CH2OH and on C3 it is the isopropyl group (each partner is H). For E they must be on opposite sides of the double bond, as in the correct structure.
x: This is the Z isomer: CH<sub>2</sub>OH and the isopropyl group are on the same side.
This is (E)-hex-2-en-1-ol, a straight chain with no methyl branch.
Here the branch is on C3 (an alkene carbon): this is 3-methylpent-2-en-1-ol.

q: What is the complete IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: The locants are {1,2} either way, so the prefix cited first alphabetically gets C1. Compare “methoxy” and “methyl” letter by letter. Then assign each center.
w: Both numberings give {1,2}. The tie goes to the prefix cited first alphabetically: m-e-t-h-o-xy comes before m-e-t-h-y-l, so the OCH3 carbon is C1. At C1: OCH3 > C2 (C,C,H) > C6 (C,H,H) > H, giving R. At C2: C1 (O,C,H) > C3 (C,H,H) > CH3 > H, also R. The two groups are trans. Name: (1R,2R)-1-methoxy-2-methylcyclohexane.
x: This is the enantiomer: both centers are inverted.
(1R,2S) is the cis diastereomer. In the drawing the groups are trans, and C2 is R.
This describes the same molecule but numbers it wrongly. With tied locants, methoxy (cited first) must get C1.

q: Which compound is a secondary amine?
h: Amines are classified by the number of carbons bonded to nitrogen, not by the kind of carbon the N is attached to.
w: Count the carbons on N. The correct choice, N-methylcyclohexanamine, has N bonded to a CH3 and a ring carbon (two carbons, one N–H): a secondary amine. This is different from alcohols, where the class depends on the carbon bearing the OH.
x: The NH<sub>2</sub> is on a carbon that has three other carbons, but the N itself bears only one carbon: this is a primary amine (1-methylcyclohexan-1-amine).
The N bears only one carbon (the CH<sub>2</sub>): cyclohexylmethanamine is a primary amine.
The N bears three carbons: N,N-dimethylcyclohexanamine is a tertiary amine.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the alkane shown?
h: Find the longest chain. Then compare the two locant sets term by term and take the set that is lower at the first point of difference.
w: The longest chain has seven carbons, running from a CH3 of the tert-butyl end to the isopropyl end. Numbering from the tert-butyl end gives substituents at {2,2,4,6}; from the other end {2,4,6,6}. At the first point of difference (second term) 2 < 4, so number from the tert-butyl end. Alphabetical order (ignoring tri-) puts ethyl first: 4-ethyl-2,2,6-trimethylheptane.
x: This numbers from the wrong end. {2,2,4,6} beats {2,4,6,6} at the second term. The sum of locants is not the rule.
Prefixes must be in alphabetical order. The multiplier “tri” is ignored, so ethyl precedes methyl.
This uses a six-carbon chain. A seven-carbon chain exists, and the longest chain is the parent.

q: A student named a compound “3-ethyl-2-methylhex-4-ene.” What is the correct IUPAC name of that compound (ignore E/Z)?
h: Draw the student's structure. The double bond must get the lowest locant, and among equally long chains the one with more substituents is the parent.
w: The student's structure is CH3–CH(CH3)–CH(C2H5)–CH=CH–CH3. The chain is right (six carbons, two substituents; the alternative six-carbon chain through the ethyl group carries only one isopropyl substituent), but it must be numbered from the end nearer the C=C. Renumbered: hex-2-ene with ethyl on C4 and methyl on C5: 4-ethyl-5-methylhex-2-ene.
x: The locants are right, but prefixes must be alphabetical: ethyl before methyl.
This chain runs through the ethyl group and carries one substituent. The equally long chain with two substituents is preferred.
This is a different compound, with the double bond moved to C2–C3 in the original numbering.

q: What is the complete IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: The parent is the longest chain (the Br carbon need not be a branch). At the stereocenter, compare CH<sub>2</sub>Br, CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub>.
w: The longest chain is four carbons and includes the CH2Br carbon, which is C1 (lowest locants {1,2}). At C2: CH2Br (Br,H,H) > CH2CH3 (C,H,H) > CH3 > H. As drawn, the center is S: (S)-1-bromo-2-methylbutane.
x: R is the mirror image. Recheck with the H pointing away: the descriptor for the drawn molecule is S.
Halogens are prefixes on the longest chain. The CH<sub>2</sub>Br carbon is part of a four-carbon chain, so it is C1, not a bromomethyl branch.
An ethyl branch on C2 means the chain was too short: the longest chain is butane.

q: Which structure is (2E,4R)-4-bromohex-2-ene?
h: Check three things in turn: Br on C4 (next to the alkene), a trans C=C, and R at C4 (Br > CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub> > CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> > H).
w: At C4 the priorities are Br > CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub> (C,C,H, counting the duplicate C for the double bond) > CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (C,H,H) > H. Only one structure has the Br on C4, a trans (E) double bond and the R configuration.
x: The double bond is Z here: the C1 methyl and C4 are on the same side.
This is the C4 epimer: the double bond is E, but C4 is S.
The Br is on C5 (two carbons from the alkene): this is (2E,5R)-5-bromohex-2-ene.

q: What is the von Baeyer name of the compound shown?
h: A fused ring system has a zero-carbon bridge. Number from a bridgehead around the largest bridge, then the next, and choose the start that gives the substituent the lowest locant.
w: Nine ring carbons, with bridges of 4, 3 and 0 carbons between the shared bridgeheads: bicyclo[4.3.0]nonane. Numbering: C1 (bridgehead), C2–C5 (four-carbon bridge), C6 (bridgehead), C7–C9 (three-carbon bridge). The methyl is on a five-ring carbon next to a bridgehead. Starting at the bridgehead not attached to it, that carbon becomes C7; the other start makes it C9. Lowest locant: 7-methylbicyclo[4.3.0]nonane (the fusion name is 1-methyloctahydro-1H-indene).
x: This starts at the other bridgehead. Both are allowed, so choose the start that gives the methyl the lower number, 7.
C8 is the middle carbon of the three-carbon bridge. The methyl is on a carbon next to a bridgehead.
Bridge lengths are cited in decreasing order: [4.3.0], not [3.4.0].

q: α-Pinene, a major component of turpentine, is shown. What is its molecular formula?
h: Count the carbons, then use rings + π bonds to find the H count: H = 2C + 2 − 2(DBE).
w: There are 10 carbons (seven in the bicyclic skeleton plus three methyls). The molecule has two rings and one C=C, so DBE = 3. H = 2(10) + 2 − 2(3) = 16. Formula: C10H16, a typical monoterpene.
x: C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>18</sub> has DBE 2. α-Pinene has two rings and a C=C, so DBE 3.
C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>14</sub> has DBE 4, one more than the two rings and one C=C present.
This misses a carbon. The gem-dimethyl bridge carbon carries two methyls, and the alkene carbon carries a third.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: In a cycloalkene the C=C carbons are C1 and C2, numbered through the double bond. Then compare the two possible substituent locant sets at the first point of difference.
w: The double-bond carbons must be C1 and C2, with numbering continuing through the C=C. Two directions are possible. If the methyl-bearing alkene carbon is C1, the methyls are at {1,6}. If the other alkene carbon is C1, the methyls are at {2,3}. At the first point of difference 1 < 2, so 1,6-dimethylcyclohex-1-ene is correct, even though {2,3} has the smaller sum.
x: The rule is first point of difference, not the smallest sum. {1,6} beats {2,3} because 1 < 2.
The double bond must be C1=C2, so “6-ene” is never correct in a cycloalkene.
In a cycloalkene the numbering runs through the C=C so it gets locants 1 and 2; a “2-ene” name with these methyl locants does not describe the drawn compound.

q: Which name breaks the IUPAC numbering rules?
h: The triple bond, as part of the parent, gets a lower locant than any substituent.
w: Draw 2-methylpent-3-yne: (CH3)2CH–C≡C–CH3. Numbering from the other end puts the triple bond at C2 instead of C3, so the correct name is 4-methylpent-2-yne. The alkyne locant takes precedence over the methyl locant. 2-Methylpent-3-yne is the incorrect name; the other three are numbered correctly.
x: HC≡C–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>: the alkyne already has locant 1, so this name is correct.
CH<sub>3</sub>C≡C–C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>: the alkyne gets 2 from this end (3 from the other), so this name is correct.
CH<sub>3</sub>C≡C–CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>: the alkyne gets 2 from this end (4 from the other), so this name is correct.

q: What is the complete IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: The OH is the suffix and gets the lowest locant. At the stereocenter, compare CH<sub>2</sub>Br with CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> by the first atoms attached.
w: The alcohol is the principal group (suffix -ol), so number to give the OH carbon the lowest locant: C2 from the CH2Br end (C3 from the other end). Bromo and methyl are prefixes: 1-bromo-3-methylbutan-2-ol. At C2: OH > CH2Br (Br,H,H) > CH(CH3)2 (C,C,H) > H, because Br outranks C at the first point of difference. As drawn the center is R: (R)-1-bromo-3-methylbutan-2-ol.
x: S is the enantiomer. Note that CH<sub>2</sub>Br outranks isopropyl even though isopropyl has more carbons.
The OH suffix must get the lowest locant (2, not 3), even if the prefixes then get higher numbers.
OH is the highest-priority group here, so it must be named as the -ol suffix, not as a hydroxy prefix.

q: Linalool, a fragrant terpene in lavender oil, is shown. Which choice correctly describes it?
c: a tertiary alcohol; 2 degrees of unsaturation
a secondary alcohol; 2 degrees of unsaturation
a tertiary alcohol; 3 degrees of unsaturation
a primary alcohol; 2 degrees of unsaturation
h: Count the carbons bonded to the C–OH carbon. For unsaturation, count rings and π bonds.
w: The OH carbon is bonded to three carbons (a CH3, the vinyl carbon and the chain CH2), so it is a tertiary alcohol (also allylic). There are no rings and two C=C bonds, so DBE = 2 (formula C10H18O: (20 + 2 − 18)/2 = 2).
x: The C–OH carbon has no H and three carbon neighbors, which makes it tertiary.
There are only two C=C bonds and no rings, so the DBE is 2.
A primary alcohol needs OH on a CH<sub>2</sub> bonded to one carbon. Here the OH carbon has three carbon neighbors.

q: A student named the compound shown “4-ethoxy-2-methylpentane.” What is the correct IUPAC name?
h: The ethoxy group is a prefix like methyl. If both directions give the same locant set, the prefix cited first alphabetically gets the lower number.
w: An ether is named as an alkoxy-substituted alkane. The parent is the five-carbon chain, with substituents at {2,4} from either end. To break the tie, the prefix cited first in alphabetical order (ethoxy) gets the lower locant: 2-ethoxy-4-methylpentane.
x: The locants are right, but prefixes must be cited alphabetically: ethoxy before methyl.
This uses a four-carbon parent. The longest chain has five carbons.
The locant sets tie ({2,4} both ways), so alphabetical order decides: ethoxy is cited first and gets 2.
